A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PaperCoder research, with matching authors, task, framework, and core experiments. Text extraction and visual inspection, including all appendices, support reliable comparison despite extensive rewriting and additions.

before.justification: v1 reports original Paper2Code and PaperBench results, author evaluations, component ablations, and manual executability checks.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds refinement experiments, reproduction tests, runtime failure analyses, and expanded human and model evaluations.

M1.justification: The default planning–analysis–coding algorithm and original generation prompts remain substantively unchanged. v4 adds experimental extensions: verification and Self-Refine of planning/analysis outputs, and execution-triggered LLM debugging (Sections 4.2–4.3; Appendix D). These introduce actual feedback and repair procedures, while remaining auxiliary to the retained generator.

E1.justification: The original 90-paper benchmark and 20-paper PaperBench Code-Dev coverage are retained. Added human-evaluation papers include trigger-free data poisoning and continual audio-video pretraining (v4 Table 20). v4 also tests a distinct incomplete-input scenario by removing Methodology sections (Table 11). Coverage expands within the existing machine-learning domain.

E2.justification: The main ChatDev, MetaGPT, Abstract, Paper, Basic Agent, and Iterative Agent comparisons remain. v4 adds a direct comparison with Self-Refine-augmented PaperCoder (Table 7). Abstract is no longer reported in the sequential component-ablation comparison (Table 6), although it remains in other comparisons. Additional backbone configurations do not constitute new baseline methods.

E3.justification: v4 adds full-rubric reproduction testing on 10 PaperBench papers and author-rubric testing on 10 human-evaluation papers, including debugging conditions and different judges. It also adds 30-paper refinement and missing-methodology protocols and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1, and o3 configurations. Human evaluation expands from 13 papers to 21 listed papers, while reporting 25 preference judgments without explaining their mapping. Execution experiments permit hardware-driven hyperparameter and data adjustments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and five-repository execution checks, v4 tests whether refinement improves downstream outputs, removes Methodology sections, stratifies performance by presentation type and research category, categorizes runtime failures, and compares reproduction with and without debugging. Its case studies now distinguish successful execution from faithful or partial reproduction (Section 4.3; Appendix B; Tables 7 and 11–16).

E5.justification: v4 newly reports three-run means and standard deviations for PaperCoder on PaperBench, except o1 and o3, and adds p≤0.05 markings and Cohen’s kappa of 0.79. Existing eight-sample judge averaging and other dispersion reporting remain. The retained Basic/Iterative Agent error bars change description from standard errors in v1 to standard deviations in v4 without explaining recalculation; significance-test details are also unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 1 scores remain unchanged. PaperCoder’s PaperBench result changes from 44.26 to a reported three-run 45.14±0.3, with additional model results; notably, o1 scores 38.31 versus Iterative Agent’s 43.3 (v4 Table 10). The expanded human study reports 88% preference and 92% helpfulness versus 77% and 85%, which are not matched-cohort gains. New reproduction, refinement, and failure results substantially expand the evidence. Code-availability and manual-edit summaries also change.

T1.justification: v4 makes the notation more explicit through prompt templates, file sets, and previously generated code context, but these restate dependencies already described in v1. Neither version supplies substantive theoretical guarantees, proofs, or derivations that are added or revised in the comparison.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central contribution: a three-stage framework generating faithful, useful repositories directly from machine-learning papers, supported by benchmark and original-author evaluations and claims of outperforming baselines. Updated headline percentages and rewritten reproduction language do not materially redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Beyond v1’s domain and proxy-evaluation caveats, v4 adds a top-down explanation of baseline differences, interpretations concerning paper underspecification and packaging failures, an explicit text-only input limitation, and concrete partial-reproduction failures. It emphasizes repositories as starting points for reproduction. Conversely, the unchanged Oracle comparison is interpreted more strongly as performance parity without significant differences, replacing v1’s acknowledgment of a remaining gap (Section 4.2).

D1.justification: v4 supplies previously absent evaluation prompts, debugging and refinement prompts, API costs, execution hardware and Docker information, debugging-model and fallback choices, and disclosures about resource-driven adjustments. Appendix A.4 newly documents generation of reproduce.sh for PaperBench. It adds a project code URL and statements about supplementary code and README instructions, and replaces the human-compensation placeholder with $15/hour. External resource availability was not verified.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Self-Refine, SciReplicate-Bench, S2ORC, ReAct, and the Transformer paper, while removing CodeT and CodeScore citations. The central positioning relative to software-development agents and PaperBench remains similar. ML-Bench is retained despite its changed author/year attribution, and publication-metadata updates do not represent new related work.

P1.justification: The method and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Previously separate experimental-setup and results sections become one Section 4 with dedicated reproduction analysis. Human-evaluation instructions move into Appendix A.2, limitations move to Appendix C, and the appendices gain an explicit hierarchy for analyses, prompts, and planning examples. This is substantial editorial reorganization beyond the added science.

P2.justification: v4 adds refinement, reproduction, failure, and cost tables; presentation/category plots; debugging examples; and planning-artifact diagrams and prompt panels. Existing displays are also reorganized: Table 1 changes conference order, the PaperBench table gains backbone columns, and executability statistics separate Python and configuration edits. Main-text panels are regrouped and the retained human-evaluation forms are resized and relocated.

improvement.justification: v1 relied chiefly on proxy scores and five manual execution checks. v4 substantially improves validation and auditability through full-rubric reproduction tests, broader runtime-failure analysis, a missing-methodology control, and complete evaluation/debugging prompts. The case studies expose the distinction between execution and faithful reproduction. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: execution settings are adjusted, Table 13’s reported average does not match its five entries, and the Oracle-parity interpretation exceeds the documented statistical support.
